cards.note: The 1909 clinical trial of compound 606 (salvarsan) is confirmed by the Nature Reviews Drug Discovery article. That article does not establish that it was the first synthetic antimicrobial cure, so origin is unknown rather than first_known.
cards.name: Salvarsan, compound 606, for syphilis
cards.summary: Ehrlich's synthetic arsenical compound 606, named salvarsan, was first tested clinically for syphilis in 1909.
cards.description: Paul Ehrlich's laboratory in Frankfurt screened derivatives up to the 606th preparation, and compound 606 was then tested against the organism that causes syphilis. The first clinical trial, in 50 patients with late-stage syphilis, was conducted in 1909 and ended with a positive outcome. The source describes this as Ehrlich's founding step in chemotherapy.
cards.origin_note: The review presents the work as the result of Ehrlich's systematic screening; it does not rank compound 606 against earlier arsenical drugs, so independence and priority are not settled.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead: a drug used widely for syphilis, and a screening method that shaped later chemotherapy as the review describes.

cards.why: Ehrlich's group screened derivatives in infected mice and then tested the most active compound against the syphilis organism, as the review describes.

events.statement: The first clinical trial of salvarsan, in 50 patients with late-stage syphilis, was conducted in 1909 and ended with a positive outcome.
events.quote: The first clinical trial of 50 patients with late-stage syphilis using salvarsan (as Ehrlich had named compound 606) was conducted in 1909, and ended with an impressive positive outcome.

open_questions: The date of the first synthesis of compound 606 and of its 1910 release were not settled by the fetched source.
The link to Prontosil (1935) and the sulfonamides was not checked.
Ehrlich's earlier dye-based work was not checked.

cards.note: The museum record cited by the source dates the Nippur prescription tablet to c. 2500 to 2340 BCE, not c. 2100 BCE, and the source's Ur III label conflicts with those dates. The c. 1050 BCE diagnostic handbook was not verified in a fetched source.
cards.name: Written medicine at Nippur
cards.summary: A Sumerian clay tablet of fifteen prescriptions from Nippur is one of the oldest known written medical texts from Mesopotamia.
cards.description: A clay tablet from Nippur, written in Sumerian, holds a collection of fifteen prescriptions. It is preserved in the University of Pennsylvania Museum and is dated c. 2500 to 2340 BCE by the record that the source cites. The later diagnostic handbook is not verified here.
cards.origin_note: The source calls the tablet one of the oldest known Mesopotamian medical texts. It does not show it was the earliest anywhere, nor how it relates to other traditions.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead, as the sources describe a scribal practice within Mesopotamia.

cards.why: The source does not state why the prescriptions were recorded.

events.label: c. 2500 to 2340 BCE
events.statement: A clay tablet from Nippur with fifteen Sumerian prescriptions is dated c. 2500 to 2340 BCE.
events.quote: Medical tablet, Iraq, Nippur, c. 2500-2340 BCE. Penn Museum No. B14221.

sources.title: One of the Oldest Known Ancient Mesopotamian Medical Texts

open_questions: The Penn Museum record (B14221) could not be fetched (403), so the date and the Ur III label need checking there.
The c. 1050 BCE diagnostic handbook (Sakikku) and its attribution to Esagil-kin-apli need a fetched source; search results gave c. 1068 to 1047 BCE.
Whether Egyptian or Greek medicine drew on Mesopotamian texts is not settled here.

cards.note: The c. 1825 BCE copy date of the Kahun papyrus is confirmed by a review table. Nothing fetched says Egyptian medicine was independent of Mesopotamia, so origin is unknown rather than independent.
cards.name: Written medicine in Egypt
cards.summary: Egyptian medical papyri set out diseases with diagnosis and treatment; the Kahun gynaecological copy is dated to about 1825 BCE.
cards.description: Egyptian medical papyri describe diseases and their treatment. The Kahun gynaecological papyrus, of which a copy is dated 1825 BCE, was found in 1889 near the Fayoum oasis. The review describes 34 sections on gynaecology, contraception and conception, with non-surgical treatments.
cards.origin_note: The sources checked describe the papyri but do not establish whether Egyptian medicine was independent of Mesopotamian medicine.

impact.note: Scores kept from the lead, as the sources describe a written medical practice within Egypt.

cards.why: The papyri record the procedures for specific cases; the source does not give a wider reason.

events.label: 1825 BCE (copy)
events.statement: A copy of the Kahun gynaecological papyrus is dated to 1825 BCE; the papyrus was found in 1889 near the Fayoum oasis.

open_questions: The earliest securely dated physician title (the lead's c. 2650 BCE) was not verified.
The Edwin Smith papyrus copy date (c. 1600 BCE) and its Old Kingdom originals are not in this card.
Transmission from Egyptian to Greek medicine was not checked.

cards.note: The sources date the Hippocratic Corpus from the fifth century BC to the second century AD, not c. 430 to 330 BCE. The Cambridge Companion says few scholars can confidently attribute even one treatise to the historical Hippocrates, so the Kos attribution is not supported.
cards.name: Hippocratic medical writings in Greece
cards.summary: A body of Greek medical treatises written from the fifth century BC on, traditionally credited to Hippocrates of Kos.
cards.description: The Hippocratic Corpus gathers about sixty treatises on medical topics, traditionally credited to Hippocrates. The sources date these works from the fifth century BC to the second century AD. The corpus mixes Coan and Cnidian material, associated with the islands of Kos and Knidos.
cards.origin_note: The sources checked do not address transmission from Egyptian or Mesopotamian practice, so the origin cannot be decided from them.

impact.note: Lead scores kept; the long influence claimed in the lead was not checked in a fetched source.

cards.why: The sources do not say why the treatises were written at this time.

events.label: 5th century BC to 2nd century AD
events.statement: The treatises of the Hippocratic Corpus were written between the fifth century BC and the second century AD.
events.quote: as the so-called Hippocratic Corpus is so diverse and contains writings from the fifth century BC to the first and second century AD

sources.title: Introduction (Chapter 1), The Cambridge Companion to Hippocrates

open_questions: Which treatises, if any, are by the historical Hippocrates is not settled; the Kos attribution needs a source.
The mid-fifth-century Cnidian treatises were not verified in a fetched source.
Egyptian and Mesopotamian influence, and the route into Roman and Arabic medicine, were not checked.

cards.note: One fetched review dates the earliest documented general hospital to Baghdad in 805 CE and says few details are known. The founder debate (Dols, possibly Yahya ibn Khalid) and the Gundeshapur model could not be checked in a fetchable source, and transmission is not shown, so origin is unknown rather than derived.
cards.name: Bimaristan hospital in Baghdad
cards.summary: The earliest documented general hospital, built in Baghdad in 805 CE by a vizier to Harun al-Rashid.
cards.description: A review records that the earliest documented general hospital was built in Baghdad in 805 CE by the vizier to Harun al-Rashid, and that few details of it are known. The Bakhtishu family of Jundishapur served as court physicians, which suggests they played a role in its development. Within a decade or two, 34 more hospitals had appeared across the Islamic world.
cards.origin_note: The review suggests a link to the Bakhtishu family of Jundishapur but does not show transmission, so a derived origin is not confirmed.

impact.note: Lead scores kept: the review reports 34 further hospitals within a decade or two, which supports a wide spread.

cards.why: The review does not give a reason for the founding.

events.label: 805 CE
events.statement: The earliest documented general hospital was built in Baghdad in 805 CE.
events.quote: The earliest documented general hospital established was built in Baghdad by the vizier to the caliph Harun al-Rashid in 805 CE.

cards.lead: The randomised controlled trial in British medicine
cards.note: The sources date publication of the MRC streptomycin trial to 1948. The 1946 start of the trial is not confirmed by a fetched source. Whether it was the first randomised trial is contested, so origin rests on the sources' phrase 'generally taken to have begun'.
cards.name: Randomised controlled trial, MRC streptomycin trial
cards.summary: The 1948 MRC streptomycin trial for tuberculosis used concealed random allocation and is generally taken to start the modern controlled trial.
cards.description: The UK Medical Research Council published its 1948 trial of streptomycin for pulmonary tuberculosis, in which patients were assigned by a concealed random process. Austin Bradford Hill, the trial's statistician, advocated this approach. Historians still debate how far it was the first randomised trial and why Hill chose randomisation.
cards.origin_note: The source says the RCT is generally taken to have begun with the 1948 MRC trial; it also notes that the claim of priority is contested.

impact.note: Lead scores kept: the review describes the method as the basis of later trial standards, and the lead's scores were not changed.

cards.why: The Part 2 review suggests Hill's advocacy of concealed random allocation followed his investigation of a failed MRC lobar pneumonia trial.

events.statement: The UK Medical Research Council's trial of streptomycin for tuberculosis, which used random allocation, was published in 1948.
events.quote: The emergence of the randomised controlled trial (RCT) as the principal means of assessing treatments is generally taken to have begun with the UK Medical Research Council (MRC) trial of streptomycin for treating tuberculosis, published in 1948

sources.title: The problematic history of randomised controlled trials Part 2: Hill's pragmatic view of randomisation and its origins
Streptomycin treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis: a Medical Research Council investigation

open_questions: Whether the trial was run in 1946 and 1947, as the lead says, is not confirmed by a fetched source.
Lind's 1747 scurvy trial and other earlier controlled comparisons were not read in a fetched source.
The location of the trial in London was not confirmed.
